questions.q: By default, who owns a securable object when it's first created?
options: Whoever created it
The metastore admin, always
The account's root user
No one; ownership must be assigned manually before use
questions.explain: Every securable object has exactly one owner, defaulting to whoever created it, and owners automatically get all privileges on that object.

questions.q: If you own a catalog, what can you do with a table inside it that you didn't personally create?
options: Manage it — ownership of a container compounds down to every child object inside it
Nothing; catalog ownership does not extend to child objects
Only read it, never modify its permissions
You must first transfer that table's ownership to yourself before managing it
questions.explain: Owning a container object (catalog or schema) automatically grants the ability to manage every object inside it, even ones you don't directly own.

questions.q: What is the correct SQL statement to transfer ownership of a table?
options: ALTER TABLE catalog.schema.table OWNER TO principal;
GRANT OWNER ON TABLE catalog.schema.table TO principal;
SET OWNER OF catalog.schema.table TO principal;
TRANSFER TABLE catalog.schema.table TO principal;
questions.explain: ALTER <securable-type> <securable-name> OWNER TO <principal> is the real Databricks syntax, e.g. ALTER TABLE finance.accounts_payable.invoices OWNER TO `accounting`;

questions.q: What restriction exists specifically for transferring ownership of a view, function, or model?
options: Only a metastore admin can transfer it to an arbitrary user; a regular owner can only transfer it to themselves or a group they belong to
Views, functions, and models can never have their ownership transferred
Only the original creator can ever own a view, permanently
Transferring view ownership requires dropping and recreating the view
questions.explain: This restriction specifically prevents privilege escalation: regular owners (or MANAGE holders) can only move view/function/model ownership to themselves or a group they're in, not to any arbitrary third party.

questions.q: Why is transferring a view's ownership to a group a common pattern?
options: It enables collaborative editing — every group member can edit the view's definition, while data access still runs through the group's own table privileges
It permanently disables all further privilege changes on that view
It is required before a view can ever be queried
It automatically converts the view into a managed table
questions.explain: Group ownership of a view lets every member of that group edit its definition collaboratively, while the data it exposes remains governed by the group's privileges on the underlying tables.
